overview.text: Affirmative action is a broad label for proactive efforts to reduce barriers and widen opportunity for groups historically excluded from education or work; it names a family of policies rather than one fixed method. In the United States, its modern federal history includes President John F. Kennedy’s 1961 order, which used the term, and a 1965 order directing federal contractors to pursue equal employment opportunity. Approaches and legal rules have varied across settings. In 2023, the Supreme Court held the race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard and the University of North Carolina unlawful under the Equal Protection Clause. That decision reshaped college admissions, but addressed those programs, not every effort called affirmative action.

key_facts.text: President John F. Kennedy’s 1961 Executive Order 10925 used “affirmative action” in connection with measures to achieve nondiscrimination.
A 1965 executive order directed federal contractors to take affirmative action to ensure equal employment opportunity.
The 1969 Philadelphia Plan used employment goals and timetables; officials distinguished those tools from quotas.
In 2023, the Supreme Court ruled that the admissions programs at Harvard and the University of North Carolina in the cases before it could not be reconciled with the Equal Protection Clause.
The Court said universities may consider an applicant’s account of how race affected their life, while requiring evaluation of the individual’s experiences rather than race itself.
